name: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar Nerve at the Elbow)
summary: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel. Elbow flexion stretches the nerve and narrows the tunnel, increasing pressure.

book.title: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar Nerve at the Elbow)

blocks.text: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel. Elbow flexion stretches the nerve and narrows the tunnel, increasing pressure. Prolonged elbow bending (phone use, sleeping with bent elbows, leaning on the elbow) provokes symptoms. It is the second most common upper limb nerve entrapment after carpal tunnel syndrome [Ref – to verify].

items: Tingling and numbness in the little finger and half of the ring finger, and the back of the hand on that side. Medial elbow ache.
In more advanced cases: clumsiness, weak pinch, wasting of the first dorsal interosseous (between thumb and index finger), clawing of the ring and little fingers.

rows: Does bending the elbow (phone, sleeping) bring it on?
Does numbness include the back of the hand?
Lesion above the wrist (cubital tunnel rather than Guyon canal)
Any neck pain or symptoms in the inner forearm?
C8 to T1 root or TOS

blocks.text: Sensation (little finger, dorsal ulnar hand, medial forearm for comparison), strength of finger abduction and pinch, observe wasting, Tinel at the cubital tunnel, elbow flexion test, Froment sign, cervical screen, ULNT3.

rows: Full elbow flexion with wrist extension, held up to 60 s
As above, with finger pressure over the nerve behind the epicondyle
Tap over the nerve in the groove
Supports nerve irritation; common in healthy people too
Patient holds paper between thumb and side of index finger while you pull
Thumb tip flexes (flexor pollicis longus substitutes for weak adductor pollicis)
Motor involvement of the ulnar nerve

blocks.label: MEMORY HOOK
body: Medial forearm numbness points to C8 to T1 or medial cutaneous nerve, not the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve does not supply the forearm skin.

rows: Guyon canal (ulnar nerve at the wrist)
Neck signs, medial forearm involved, thumb flexor weakness

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Wasting with fasciculations, no sensory loss

steps: **Ulnar sensory symptoms, positive elbow flexion test, no progressive motor loss:** working diagnosis mild to moderate cubital tunnel syndrome. Start conservative care.
**Weakness or wasting, or no improvement after about 3 months:** refer for nerve conduction studies and surgical opinion.

items: **Education and activity change (main treatment)**: avoid prolonged elbow flexion and leaning on the elbow; use a headset for phone calls.

**Night splint or towel wrap**: keep the elbow at about 30 to 45 degrees of flexion while sleeping [Ref – to verify]. **Nerve sliders**: gentle ulnar nerve gliding (Vol 13 Ch 5), no strong tensioning.

blocks.text: Symptom frequency, elbow flexion test time to symptoms, pinch strength, intrinsic strength, wasting.

items: **Why does phone use worsen symptoms?** Sustained elbow flexion compresses and stretches the ulnar nerve.
**What does a positive Froment sign show?** Weak adductor pollicis from ulnar motor involvement.
**Dorsal ulnar hand sensation is normal, little finger numb. Where is the lesion?** Likely at the wrist (Guyon canal).
**When should you refer for surgery?** Progressive weakness or wasting, or no improvement after adequate conservative care.
**Why sliders rather than tensioners?** Less provocation of a sensitive nerve.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Localise ulnar nerve symptoms to the elbow, wrist or neck.
Perform elbow flexion, Tinel and Froment tests.
Plan conservative care and know when to refer.
